Catherine Flon

Biography

Introduction

Catherine Flon is a name etched into the very fabric of Haitian national identity. She is celebrated across the republic and its diaspora as the woman who stitched together the first Haitian flag during the crucial Congress of Arcahaie in May 1803 [1]. While popular history often simplifies her contribution to that of a patriotic seamstress—frequently drawing comparisons to Betsy Ross of the American Revolution—her role was deeply woven into the broader military, social, and political mobilization of the Haitian Revolution. As the goddaughter of the revolutionary commander Jean-Jacques Dessalines, Flon operated not merely as an isolated artisan, but as an active participant in the liberation struggle, running a workshop that doubled as a training ground for young women and a support hub for the indigenous army [2]. Her legacy represents the vital, yet frequently marginalized, contributions of women who served as nurses, spies, and coordinators in the world's only successful slave revolution.

Early Life and the Colonial Crucible of Saint-Domingue

Catherine Flon was born on December 2, 1772, in the coastal town of Arcahaie, located in the western province of what was then the French colony of Saint-Domingue [1]. At the time of her birth, Saint-Domingue was the wealthiest and most brutally exploitative colony in the Caribbean, often referred to as the "Pearl of the Antilles." Its immense wealth, derived from sugar, coffee, indigo, and cotton, was sustained by the forced labor of hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans under a regime of terror codified by the Code Noir.

Flon was born into the class of gens de couleur libres (free people of color), a group that occupied a complex social tier between the ruling white colonists (grands blancs and petits blancs) and the vast population of enslaved Black laborers. Her parents were successful merchants and tradespeople involved in the textile trade, owning a relatively prosperous workshop in Arcahaie [2][3]. This background allowed Catherine to receive training in fine needlework, tailoring, and fabric manipulation—skills that were rare and highly valued in the colonial economy.

As the French Revolution of 1789 began to destabilize the colonial order, tensions between Saint-Domingue's racial and class factions erupted. In August 1791, the massive slave uprising sparked by the ceremony at Bois Caïman transformed the colony into a war zone. Seeing the writing on the wall, many free people of color and white colonists began to flee. Catherine's parents ultimately chose to leave Saint-Domingue for France to escape the violence [3]. Catherine, however, refused to abandon her homeland. She remained in Arcahaie, took ownership of the family workshop, and converted it into an independent enterprise where she taught young girls, particularly free women of color and newly liberated Black girls, the art of sewing and design [2].

The Rise of the Revolution and Quiet Resistance

Throughout the 1790s, the revolution evolved through multiple phases, marked by the rise of Toussaint Louverture and the abolition of slavery by the French National Convention in 1794. During this period of relative stability under Louverture's leadership, Arcahaie remained a critical strategic point. Flon's workshop flourished, but it also became a site of covert political organization [2].

The situation deteriorated rapidly in 1802 when Napoleon Bonaparte dispatched a massive French expeditionary force led by his brother-in-law, General Charles Leclerc, with the secret mission of disarming the local forces and restoring slavery. The arrest and subsequent deportation of Toussaint Louverture in June 1802 shattered any remaining illusions of reconciliation with France. The revolutionary leadership fell to Louverture's top generals, most notably Jean-Jacques Dessalines, Henri Christophe, and Alexandre Pétion [3].

As the conflict escalated into a war of total independence, Flon’s role transformed. She was the goddaughter of Jean-Jacques Dessalines, who placed great trust in her intelligence and discretion [1][2]. Her workshop in Arcahaie was repositioned to support the revolutionary army. Under her guidance, the young women of her workshop produced bandages, military uniforms, and bags for carrying ammunition [2]. Moreover, Flon and her apprentices worked as nurses, establishing a makeshift hospital in Arcahaie to treat soldiers wounded in conflicts along the western coast [2][3]. This work was highly dangerous, as the French army under Leclerc (and later the notoriously brutal General Rochambeau) routinely executed anyone suspected of aiding the revolutionary forces.

"She did not merely stitch bands of cloth; she wove the spirit of an undivided nation, binding the destiny of a free people to the colors of liberty." — Historical commentary on the creation of the Haitian flag [4].

The Congress of Arcahaie and the Creation of the Flag

By early 1803, the war had reached a fever pitch. General Rochambeau waged a genocidal campaign, employing torture and mass executions to terrorize the population. This brutality forced a historic alignment. Historically divided by race, class, and regional rivalries, the Black forces led by Dessalines and the Mulatto forces led by Alexandre Pétion realized that they had to unite or face total annihilation.

From May 15 to May 18, 1803, the revolutionary leaders convened in Arcahaie for a historic summit known as the Congress of Arcahaie [1]. The goal was to establish a unified military command and define a common national symbol that would represent their alliance. The French tricolor flag, which the revolutionary forces had previously carried to show their nominal loyalty to the ideals of the French Republic, was no longer appropriate.

On May 18, 1803, the climax of the congress occurred. In a dramatic public gesture, Jean-Jacques Dessalines took a French tricolor flag, placed it on a table, and ripped out the white center band [1][5]. The white band represented the French colonizers, and its removal symbolized the complete rejection of French colonial authority. Dessalines then presented the remaining blue and red bands to his goddaughter, Catherine Flon, and commanded her to sew them together [1][5].

Flon took the two strips of cloth and stitched them together. The blue strip was placed at the top, representing the Black population of Haiti, while the red strip was placed at the bottom, representing the Mulatto population [1][5]. According to oral tradition, the sewing was done using Flon’s own hair as thread to reinforce the bond, symbolizing the permanent and unbreakable union between the two groups. Other versions of the story suggest she used her needlework to stitch the words "Liberté ou la Mort" (Liberty or Death) or "L'Union fait la force" (Unity makes strength) onto the fabric [5]. The creation of the flag was met with immense celebration by the assembled troops, serving as a powerful catalyst for the final push against the French.

The Triumph of Independence and Post-Revolutionary Years

The unity forged at Arcahaie bore fruit on November 18, 1803, when the indigenous army defeated the French at the Battle of Vertières, forcing the evacuation of the remaining French forces. On January 1, 1804, in the city of Gonaïves, Jean-Jacques Dessalines read the Declaration of Independence, officially renaming the colony Haiti—the original Taíno name for the island.

Following the declaration of independence, Haiti entered a tumultuous period of state-building. Dessalines was declared Emperor Jacques I in late 1804 but was assassinated in 1806, leading to a civil war that divided the country into the Northern Kingdom under Henri Christophe and the Southern Republic under Alexandre Pétion.

Throughout these turbulent decades, Catherine Flon chose to live a quiet life in Arcahaie [1]. She resisted invitations to move to the imperial or royal courts, preferring to continue her work as a seamstress and teacher. She remained a beloved figure in her community, recognized as a living monument to the birth of the nation. She died in Arcahaie in 1831 at the age of 58 [1][3].

Legacy and Modern Commemoration

Catherine Flon is revered today as one of Haiti's greatest national heroes. Her legacy is celebrated annually on May 18, which is observed throughout Haiti and its diaspora as Haitian Flag Day (Fête du Drapeau) [1]. On this day, schools, civic organizations, and community groups host parades, cultural events, and discussions centered on the theme of unity that Flon’s flag represents.

Her contribution was formally recognized by the Haitian government in 2000 when her likeness was placed on the 10-gourde banknote, making her the first woman to be featured on Haitian currency [6]. In public schools across Haiti, she is taught as a symbol of female patriotism and courage.

Historians and feminist scholars also view Catherine Flon as a critical window into the lives of women in the Haitian Revolution. While colonial archives largely ignored women—focusing instead on the military exploits of men like Louverture, Dessalines, and Christophe—oral histories and local traditions preserved the memory of figures like Flon, Sanité Bélair, and Cécile Fatiman. Her story serves as a reminder that the Haitian Revolution was not won by soldiers alone, but by a collective societal mobilization in which women played indispensable roles.

Major Contributions

Catherine Flon's primary contribution to Caribbean history was her creation of the first Haitian flag during the Congress of Arcahaie in May 1803. By stitching together the blue and red bands after the removal of the white stripe from the French tricolor, she produced a powerful national symbol of unity between the Black and Mulatto populations, which was essential for the successful completion of the Haitian Revolution. Beyond her symbolic role as the nation's seamstress, Flon was a crucial community leader and caregiver. She operated a sewing workshop in Arcahaie that trained young women of color, served as a dedicated nurse tending to wounded soldiers in the indigenous army, and provided vital logistical support to the revolutionary forces led by her godfather, Jean-Jacques Dessalines.
